items.summary: With an estimated 36% of people in the United States having some degree of lactose intolerance, there may be an expanded market for lactose-free or reduced-lactose ice cream—especially if those with lactose intolerance are willing to pay more for such products, according to a study led by researcher

items.title: Learning style predicts survival skills in young orangutans
items.summary: Orangutan infants spend their first eight years with their mothers, and throughout this time, they can draw on their knowledge. items.title: New catalogs map the quantum possibilities of atomically thin materials
items.summary: Twistronics has become a new alchemy of materials. By choosing atomically thin layers, stacking them and changing their relative angle, researchers can create electronic behavior absent from the original ingredients. items.title: A new venomous British snake? Why there's no need to panic
items.summary: Great Britain has long been thought to be home to a single venomous snake species, the adder. Although its bites are rarely life-threatening, they require a trip to the emergency department and will more than likely ruin your week. items.title: New AlphaFold Database release adds viral protein complexes to support pandemic preparedness
items.summary: AI-predicted protein complex structures for more than 2,800 viruses are now openly available in the AlphaFold Database. To better understand and protect against emerging pathogens, the dataset prioritizes proteomes from viral families known to infect humans.

items.title: Sharks can hear sounds nearly 250 feet away and find the source
items.summary: Sound travels through the ocean carrying clues about potential prey, predators and other animals, giving sharks an important way to detect what they cannot yet see. items.title: Is the universe twisted? A new check on a possible twist in the universe's oldest light
items.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the universe's oldest light, leftover thermal radiation from about 380,000 years after the big bang. Maps of the CMB offer a picture of the "baby universe" as it was 13.8 billion years ago.

items.title: Greenland ice shelf weakened by estuary ahead of recent calving event
items.summary: In August 2026, an iceberg the size of Manhattan broke away from the Petermann Ice Shelf in northern Greenland. It was the glacier's largest calving event since 2020. items.title: In Alaska, wildfires help prevent future burns. Researchers question if that feedback loop will hold
items.summary: In Alaska's boreal forests, a negative feedback loop between wildfires and vegetation plays an important role in governing the size and likelihood of fires. Wildfires clear out mature forests, allowing them to be replaced by less flammable young forests that temporarily suppress fires. This rel

items.title: Montreal's squirrels provide insight into evolutionary change in urban species
items.summary: By comparing variations in the coat colors of eastern gray squirrels (Sciurus carolinensis) in Montreal city parks, researchers found that hyperlocal conditions appear to play a bigger role in shaping wildlife traits than previously thought.

items.title: New ways to protect crops by targeting pathogen weaknesses
items.summary: Scientists from the Biosciences Department at Durham University have outlined possible new approaches to protecting crops from devastating diseases by finding common weaknesses in the proteins pathogens use to attack plants. The researchers presented their ideas in a recent review article in The Pla

items.title: Hurricane Polo triggers huge waves in coastal Mexican city
items.summary: Hurricane Polo swirled menacingly along Mexico's southern coast Thursday, triggering towering waves in a Pacific port city.

items.summary: Carbon-capture technology repurposed for breweries spreads and finds new applications

items.title: Family resilience can help protect children from climate change
items.summary: As climate change brings more extreme weather events, strengthening families before disasters strike can help protect children's health and well-being, says Mary McKay, a professor at the Brown School at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on child mental health.

items.title: Mistletoe berry glue bonds even nonstick Teflon and can be reactivated with heat
items.summary: Mistletoe is best known from winter traditions as a symbol of luck and affection. For trees, however, the hemiparasitic plant can be a burden: It draws water and nutrients from its hosts. Now the plant could provide a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based industrial adhesives.

items.summary: In this Aug. 27, 2026, image, an Alta-X drone flies an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. items.title: Supernova or black hole: Neutrino 'flavor' may determine the fate of dying stars
items.summary: As a star nears the end of its life, it faces two very different fates: It can explode as a supernova, leaving behind a neutron star, or collapse and become a black hole. What determines the outcome remains one of astrophysics' great unanswered questions.

items.title: Major survey reveals public support for UK nature recovery
items.summary: A new survey from the University of Exeter and the University of Surrey reveals broad public support for policies to protect and restore nature in the U.K. Researchers surveyed almost 3,000 people across the country, exploring their feelings, concerns, opinions and experiences in nature.

items.title: Scientists reconstruct one of this century's most explosive volcanic eruptions to explore its role in a tsunami
items.summary: In 2022, the eruption and collapse of an underwater volcano in Tonga caused a devastating tsunami that killed four people, disrupted seafloor ecosystems and damaged critical seafloor telecommunications cables. It was one of the most powerful volcanic events this century.
